1.1.title: Study without inventing
1.1.prompt: You meet an unfamiliar claim in a lesson. What should you do before trying to answer a study question about it?
1.1.options: Read the relevant source, hide it, then rebuild the meaning in your own words||Guess the meaning from the field name, then keep going if it sounds confident||Reread the same paragraph several times until its wording feels familiar||Ask an AI for the answer without giving it the source or the target version
1.1.explanation: Reading the relevant part first gives you an accurate definition to work from. Hiding it and rebuilding the meaning tests understanding; comparing afterward catches what you got wrong.

1.2.title: Follow one choice
1.2.prompt: The input is 100 and the action is spend. In the lesson's add-or-subtract example, which result does the branch choose?
1.2.options: 99, because the branch follows the subtract_one path for spend||101, because both add_one and subtract_one run for every action||100, because a branch only reads the input and cannot change it||0, because the CPU clears the input once the action is compared
1.2.explanation: The branch compares the action with its choices and follows the subtract path for spend. subtract_one changes 100 to 99; the add path is not taken.

1.3.title: Update several players
1.3.prompt: Why keep Ada and Bo as player records in a collection when both collect one coin?
1.3.options: One loop can apply the same gold update to each player's record||Their gold fields must sit at the same memory address in RAM||Their health values must stay equal so one rule can handle both||The shop's screen text then becomes the rule that sets the price
1.3.explanation: Each record groups one player's fields. A loop visits each record and applies the same one-coin rule, even when the collection grows.

1.4.title: Check before spending
1.4.prompt: A player has 10 gold and an item costs 25. What does `spend_if_possible(10, 25)` return?
1.4.options: 10, because the gold is below the cost, so the subtraction is skipped||0, because the function spends every coin the player currently has||25, because the function returns the item's cost whenever it is called||-15, because 10 minus 25 is computed and returned as the new gold
1.4.explanation: The function subtracts only when gold is at least the cost. With 10 and 25, that condition is false, so it returns the unchanged gold amount, 10.

1.5.title: Read Mira, then change stamina
1.5.prompt: Why does the Rust primer call `show_stamina(&mira)` but `dash(&mut mira, 4)`?
1.5.options: The first only reads Mira, while the second needs temporary permission to change her||The first copies Mira into the function, while the second builds a brand new runner||Both calls permanently hand Mira over, so `main` can no longer use her afterward||The `&mut` form tells `dash` that the stamina cost it receives is a negative number
1.5.explanation: `&mira` lends read access to the existing runner. `&mut mira` lends editable access for the dash call. Mira remains owned by `main` and can be read again after `dash` returns.

1.6.title: Change one variable
1.6.prompt: Why should a memory experiment change one game behavior at a time?
1.6.options: The observed byte difference then has one clearer possible cause||The change freezes every other process, so only one value can move||The address you found becomes stable for every future run of the game||The repeat test becomes unnecessary, since a single change proves the cause
1.6.explanation: A controlled change narrows cause and effect; repeating it shows whether the same change gives the same result.

1.7.title: Protect the experiment
1.7.prompt: Why take a virtual-machine snapshot before a memory or debugger lab?
1.7.options: It gives you a known recovery point to return to after a mistake or crash||It keeps every address in the game fixed so later scans give the same results||It gives the guest Windows unlimited permissions inside your main computer||It stops the game from changing its state while you debug it in the lab
1.7.explanation: A snapshot captures a controlled machine state that can be restored. It does not freeze future addresses or remove normal operating-system protections.

1.8.title: Separate where from what
1.8.prompt: In the lesson's numbered-box model, what does an address tell you?
1.8.options: Which location to read in that process||The value's type and meaning by itself||The name of the original source-code variable||How long the object will live
1.8.explanation: An address identifies where to look in a process. The bytes there need a type and the program's use of them before they become a meaningful value.

1.9.title: Use a controlled change
1.9.prompt: A first scan finds many addresses containing 100. You recruit a unit and the visible gold changes to 85. Which addresses should the next scan inspect?
1.9.options: Only the first scan's candidates, keeping those now holding 85||Every address in the whole process, searched again from scratch||Only the executable code regions, since gold is changed by code||Only the lowest address from the first scan, as the likeliest
1.9.explanation: A value scan is an iterative filtering algorithm. Each controlled change narrows the existing candidate set instead of starting over from the whole process.

2.1.title: Explain the pause
2.1.prompt: What useful fact does a breakpoint provide during a controlled game experiment?
2.1.options: Which instruction or access caused the pause, plus the state to inspect||The permanent address of every object the game will ever create||The original source-code variable name for the value being watched||Proof that the paused instruction explains all the related behavior
2.1.explanation: A breakpoint gives a controlled observation near an instruction or watched access. A data watchpoint may report after the write, so inspect the debugger's stop reason and current state. Repeating the same action strengthens the connection to the behavior.

2.2.title: Follow the names
2.2.prompt: A release game has no debug information for its `health` field. Why can the code still read that field without its source name?
2.2.options: The compiler fixed the layout, so the code uses the field's offset from the object base||The linker stripped every name, and Windows reads each field by its position||Windows restores the field name from a hidden table when the game starts||The compiler encrypted the name inside the instruction so only the CPU can read it
2.2.explanation: The compiled instruction can use the field's distance from the object base without referring to `health` by name. Separate debug information may still preserve source names, and an executable may retain import or export names. A missing source name does not imply obfuscation.

2.3.title: Read the instruction
2.3.prompt: In `mov eax, [rcx+8]`, what do the brackets mean?
2.3.options: Read the value stored in memory at address rcx plus 8||Add eight to the register named rcx, with no memory read||Jump to the function located eight bytes after rcx||Store the text "rcx+8" into the register eax
2.3.explanation: Brackets indicate a memory operand. The CPU calculates the address, then loads the bytes found there.

2.4.title: Pause and inspect
2.4.prompt: What is the main purpose of a breakpoint in a reversing experiment?
2.4.options: Pause one path so registers, memory, and the stack can be read||Permanently change the game so the paused code never runs again||Encrypt an instruction so that only the debugger can run it||Make a pointer valid by filling in its missing address
2.4.explanation: A breakpoint stops one thread at a chosen moment so its registers, memory, and call stack can be read, without making the paused state permanent.

2.5.title: Watch the data, not one function
2.5.prompt: Why use a hardware write breakpoint on the gold address?
2.5.options: It can reveal any instruction that writes the watched bytes||It permanently patches the subtraction instruction in place||It converts the gold value into a pointer for the debugger||It pauses only when one specific function is called
2.5.explanation: A data breakpoint watches an address range. Different code paths can trigger it, which makes it useful when you know the changing data before you know the responsible instruction.

2.6.title: Climb toward the cause
2.6.prompt: How does the call stack help trace a low-level gold write back toward a menu action?
2.6.options: Return addresses show the chain of callers that led here||It stores every gold value that was used since launch||It contains the source code for each active function||It records all CPU instructions permanently as they run
2.6.explanation: Stack frames and return addresses describe active function calls. Walking upward moves from the immediate write toward the higher-level decision that requested it.

2.7.title: Describe a moving address
2.7.prompt: What location description normally survives ASLR for one exact module build?
2.7.options: The current module base plus a build-specific RVA||One absolute address copied down from yesterday's run||The title shown on the game's window while it runs||The process ID that Windows gave the game this time
2.7.explanation: ASLR moves the base, while an RVA identifies a distance inside that same module build.

2.8.title: Prove stability
2.8.prompt: What is the strongest evidence that a pointer path is useful?
2.8.options: The pinned build's starting address and dereference steps resolve the intended object across clean restarts||The final address it produces is a small number with few digits, which makes it easy to type and compare||The chain resolved correctly once in one session, and the gold value matched the screen at that moment||Every link in the chain adds the same offset, which shows the objects follow a regular repeating layout
2.8.explanation: This lab starts from a build-specific absolute address, then follows offsets and dereferences. Clean restarts test whether that path remains useful in the pinned build. A separately verified module base plus RVA would be a more portable starting design.

2.9.title: Return safely
2.9.prompt: Where should a code-cave detour return after replaying displaced behavior?
2.9.options: The first complete original instruction after the overwritten region||The middle of the last instruction that was overwritten by the jump||The first byte of the jump that was written at the hook site||The start of the whole function that contains the hook site
2.9.explanation: Returning at a verified instruction boundary preserves the decoder's byte stream and original control flow.

2.10.title: Leave the machine as you found it
2.10.prompt: A code cave adds one instruction that changes `eax` and the flags, then replays the displaced instructions and jumps back. Why must it save and restore `eax` and the flags around its own work?
2.10.options: The hooked function was mid-calculation, so later instructions may still need the values in `eax` and the flags||The debugger stops the cave when any register differs from the value it had at the first breakpoint it set||The jump back to the return address cannot run until the flags hold the values they had at program start||Windows restores the registers it considers volatile, so the cave must save the remaining ones itself
2.10.explanation: The hook interrupts a function in the middle of its work, so registers, flags, and stack entries may already hold values its later instructions depend on. If the cave leaves `eax` or the flags changed, the original code keeps running with the wrong inputs, and the failure may only show up later, which is why a hook can seem to work once and then crash.

3.1.title: Contain the assumption
3.1.prompt: Why should raw-pointer and Win32 FFI work live in a small Rust boundary?
3.1.options: The assumptions can be documented in one place, and callers can use checked types||Code inside the wrapper is verified automatically by the compiler once it is marked||Windows API calls begin to return errors inside a wrapper written this way||Raw pointers handled by the wrapper are given permanent lifetimes by the compiler
3.1.explanation: A narrow boundary makes validity rules reviewable and keeps most of the program in ordinary safe Rust.

3.2.title: Explain the bias
3.2.prompt: Why does an `f32` store its exponent with 127 added instead of storing the power of two directly?
3.2.options: So an eight-bit field with no minus sign can still hold negative powers of two||So the number takes up less memory than it would with a plain signed exponent||Because 127 is the largest value that a single byte of memory is able to hold||So the CPU can skip reading the fraction bits when the exponent is a small one
3.2.explanation: The field only holds 0 to 255. Storing the real exponent plus 127 lets the stored values 1 to 254 stand for real exponents −126 to 127, and the reader subtracts 127 to get the power of two back.

3.3.title: Respect the process boundary
3.3.prompt: What should an external Rust observer do with a target-process field?
3.3.options: Copy bounded bytes through the operating-system API into a local typed value||Cast the remote address to a local reference and read the field through it||Assume each read returned the whole range without checking the byte count||Request write access for every observation so the read cannot be refused
3.3.explanation: Another process owns the address. A checked copy keeps that boundary and its failure modes explicit.

3.4.title: Separate an address from an offset
3.4.prompt: A player object begins at `0x12340000`, and a method reads yaw from `[ecx+0x40]` while `ecx` holds that object. Which address contains yaw?
3.4.options: `0x12340040`, the object base plus the `0x40` offset||`0x00000040`, because the offset alone names the field||`0x123399C0`, the object base minus the `0x40` offset||The first function address in the object's vtable table
3.4.explanation: The object base is the starting address and `0x40` is the byte distance to the member, so the field address is `0x12340000 + 0x40 = 0x12340040`.

3.5.title: Recognize a vptr
3.5.prompt: Which observation most strongly supports a suspected C++ vptr?
3.5.options: The object starts with a pointer to a read-only table whose entries lead to executable methods||The object's first byte is nonzero, and the object itself is stored in the heap region||The object's first field is a number that changes whenever the player moves around||A string found near the object in the module contains the word player in its text
3.5.explanation: A pointer from the object to a read-only table whose entries lead to executable methods matches how compilers commonly implement virtual dispatch. It shows the object has virtual methods; it does not recover the class name.

3.6.title: Reject a stale identity
3.6.prompt: What does the generation part of an index-plus-generation handle prove?
3.6.options: The slot still represents the same logical object generation||The slot's object has a permanent address in memory||The container is encrypted so that other tools cannot read it||The handle owns the process that created the object
3.6.explanation: A reused slot increments its generation, so an older handle cannot silently resolve to a different object.

3.7.title: Test the transformation
3.7.prompt: What property should a reversible toy value transform satisfy over many inputs?
3.7.options: decode(encode(value, key), key) gives back value||encode(value, key) stays equal to zero each time||the key is kept inside every encoded value||one sample happens to decode plausibly once
3.7.explanation: A round-trip property checks that the proposed inverse really undoes the complete transform rather than fitting one coincidence.

3.8.title: Interpret text bytes
3.8.prompt: Why is finding readable text in memory not enough to identify a complete string?
3.8.options: You also need its encoding, its length rule or terminator, and its lifetime||All text is stored encrypted, so readable bytes could only be a partial decoy copy||Each character occupies exactly four bytes, so readable bytes are always a fragment||Strings are always moved right after allocation, so any address you find is stale
3.8.explanation: Bytes become text only under an encoding and boundary rule. FFI code must also respect whether the memory stays valid while another API reads it.

4.1.title: Where does the rule live?
4.1.prompt: In Wesnoth you change one unit's hit points in memory. You then recruit another unit of the same type. What hit points does the new unit have, and why?
4.1.options: The WML file's value, because each new unit is built from the definition on disk||The edited value, because a memory edit applies to every unit of that type at once||Zero, because the memory edit corrupted the stored definition of the unit type||A random value, because recruiting a unit reloads the whole game from scratch
4.1.explanation: A memory edit changes one object in one running match. In this example, each new recruit gets its starting value from the WML definition. Editing that definition affects later recruits loaded from it; Chapter 9 explores file edits. Knowing where a rule lives helps predict how long a change will last.

4.2.title: Does an identical write count?
4.2.prompt: A tool writes 100 into a character's health on every frame, and the health is already 100. A health-bar system asks the engine for the entities whose health changed. What does that system receive?
4.2.options: The character every frame, since a write stamps the component even when the value is equal||Nothing, since the engine compares the values and finds no difference between them||The character once, on the first write only, until the value really differs||The character only when the new value is below 100, since only drops count
4.2.explanation: Change detection compares stamps, not values. Each write stamps the component with the current counter, so every system triggered by a change runs on every frame. A system that was skipped for a while still sees every change since its own last run, because it compares against its own counter.

4.3.title: Observe before deciding
4.3.prompt: Why should a strategy-game observer build one validated snapshot before running rules?
4.3.options: The rules get one coherent model, not scattered reads of changing memory||It makes the game server trust the tool, since a snapshot carries a signature||It removes map boundaries, since a snapshot stores every tile as visible||It keeps the data fresh, since a snapshot updates itself as the game runs
4.3.explanation: Collection and validation belong in one layer; strategy can then work with meaningful bounded data.

4.4.title: Revalidate before writing
4.4.prompt: When should a captured remote address gain authority to become a write destination?
4.4.options: Only after the profile, object path, current value, and fresh precondition all still agree||As soon as the address is nonzero, since zero is the only invalid address||Whenever the same number appears elsewhere in memory during the same scan||After the tool requests full process access, since write rights then include the path
4.4.explanation: An address is valid only for the run and object it came from. A guarded action re-checks the target and object path immediately before the narrow write, then checks the result.

4.5.title: Locate one tile
4.5.prompt: A row-major visibility map is `width` tiles wide. Which formula finds tile `(x, y)` in a flat array?
4.5.options: y × width + x||x × height + y||width ÷ y + x||x + y + width
4.5.explanation: Each completed row contributes `width` elements. Adding `x` then selects the column within row `y`.

4.6.title: Make automation explainable
4.6.prompt: Why model an offline macro as named states and guarded transitions?
4.6.options: The current action, allowed next actions, and stop behavior become explicit and testable||It makes input timing unnecessary, since each state waits for the right moment itself||It guarantees the game accepts every action, since a state cannot be rejected by the game||It removes the need to observe game state, since each transition is already known
4.6.explanation: A finite-state machine turns an implicit loop into inspectable rules. That makes timeouts, cancellation, and unexpected observations easier to handle safely.

4.7.title: Picture the vector
4.7.prompt: What does target position minus observer position produce?
4.7.options: A displacement arrow from the observer toward the target||A pixel position where the target appears on screen||A single distance value with the direction thrown away||A new point halfway between observer and target
4.7.explanation: Subtracting positions removes the shared origin and leaves direction plus distance between the points.

4.8.title: Separate observation from decision
4.8.prompt: Why should a coordinate bot first copy game data into a validated snapshot?
4.8.options: Decision logic can work from one bounded, internally consistent model||The snapshot stays a live pointer, so decisions see updates instantly||Copying makes the coordinates permanent inside the game itself||With a snapshot, the bot no longer needs any stop conditions
4.8.explanation: Remote state can change during a read. A validated snapshot gives movement code a clear input and keeps memory-access failures out of steering logic.

4.9.title: Choose a search rule
4.9.prompt: Why does breadth-first search find a shortest route on a grid where every legal move has equal cost?
4.9.options: It visits tiles in order of their step count from the start||It steers toward the goal coordinates at every single step||It inspects every tile in the whole map before it picks a route||It treats wall tiles as walkable until a route has been found
4.9.explanation: A FIFO frontier visits every distance-one node before distance-two nodes, so the first reached goal uses the fewest equal-cost edges.

4.10.title: React once
4.10.prompt: Why diff two accepted snapshots before sending them to a bot state machine?
4.10.options: It turns repeated polled values into one-time change events||It keeps the remote game memory permanent between each pair of polls||It removes the need for any timeout or cooldown on later actions||It presses the matching input key automatically after each change
4.10.explanation: A snapshot states what is true now; a diff identifies what changed, preventing one transition from firing on every poll.

4.11.title: Move only owned facts
4.11.prompt: What should a debugger copy into an asynchronous telemetry event?
4.11.options: Small owned values such as timestamps, thread IDs, and relative addresses||A borrowed pointer to one field inside the current DEBUG_EVENT union||The live process handle, so the writer thread can close it afterward||A complete copy of the target's stack so the log can be replayed later
4.11.explanation: The event-handling scope owns temporary Windows data and must continue promptly. Compact owned facts can safely outlive that scope and be formatted by another thread.

4.12.title: Why the edit does not stick
4.12.prompt: In your own offline toy, a guard has been chasing a player it has seen for five ticks in a row. You write 0 (Patrol) into its state byte between two ticks. What happens on the next tick, and why?
4.12.options: It chases again, because `decide` rebuilds the state and `seen_for` is 3 or more||It patrols from then on, because the state is chosen only once, at the start||It crashes at once, because 0 is not a valid value for any guard's state||It attacks the player, because Patrol wraps round to the next state in the list
4.12.explanation: The state is an output that `decide` rebuilds from the senses every tick. `seen_for` is still at least `REACTION_TICKS` = 3, so Patrol turns straight back into Chase before the act stage runs. An edit lasts only when the inputs agree with it, or when it changes an input the rules read, such as health.

4.13.title: Where the choice flips
4.13.prompt: A fighter sees an enemy, has no cover, and has no potions left. It scores Attack as 0.4 + 0.6 × h and Take cover as 0.9 − 0.6 × h, where h is its health as a fraction of full health. Below what health does it stop attacking and take cover, and why?
4.13.options: About 0.42, where 0.4 + 0.6h = 0.9 − 0.6h gives 1.2h = 0.5||0.5, since half health is the point where utility systems switch||0.25, since that is the point where healing starts to win||It does not switch, since Attack scores at least 0.4 at any health
4.13.explanation: Utility scoring runs whichever option scores highest, so the choice flips where the two lines cross. Adding 0.6h to both sides of 0.4 + 0.6h = 0.9 − 0.6h and taking 0.4 from both gives 1.2h = 0.5, so h = 0.5 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 0.42. Above that health Attack scores more; below it Take cover does. With no potions, Heal scores 0, so the 0.25 switch point never comes into play. Changing one number in either formula moves the crossing, which is how designers tune utility AI.

5.1.title: Use the correct coordinate system
5.1.prompt: Why is a PE RVA not always the same number as a file offset?
5.1.options: A section's place in memory can differ from its place on disk||An RVA is the process ID, which changes with every run||Executable files have no headers, so the numbers are guessed||Windows places every section at address zero in the live image
5.1.explanation: The section table maps locations in the loaded image to locations in the on-disk file.

5.2.title: Relocate the symbol
5.2.prompt: A symbol has RVA `0x2500` and the module loaded at `0x7FF600000000`. How is its live address found?
5.2.options: Add the RVA to the live module base||Subtract the live base from the RVA||Take the file offset as an absolute pointer||Multiply the RVA by the live module base
5.2.explanation: An RVA is a distance from the image base. ASLR changes the live base, while the RVA remains tied to that exact module build.

5.3.title: Map an exported function
5.3.prompt: When parsing a DLL file on disk, why can an export RVA not always be used directly as a file offset?
5.3.options: An RVA measures the loaded image, so the section's virtual and raw ranges must be used to convert it||An RVA is stored in a compressed form, so it must be expanded by the loader before any bytes are read||Exports live only in RAM after loading, so no offset exists for them inside the file on disk||Every section starts at file offset zero, so an RVA must be shifted by the section count first
5.3.explanation: PE sections can have different raw-file and virtual positions. A bounded section mapping converts an RVA into the correct file location.

5.4.title: Match stable bytes
5.4.prompt: Why does a byte pattern use wildcards for some positions?
5.4.options: Displacements or addresses may vary between builds while the surrounding opcode structure stays meaningful||Wildcards tell the CPU to skip those bytes, so the scan finishes faster than an exact comparison||Wildcards let the pattern match any module in the process, which removes the need to pick a build||Wildcards turn off address randomization for the bytes they cover, so the match stays in place
5.4.explanation: A good signature anchors the stable context and treats relocation-sensitive bytes as unknown. Wildcards relax equality; they do not change what the CPU executes.

5.5.title: Narrow the candidates
5.5.prompt: Why compare scan candidates after a controlled value change?
5.5.options: Only addresses that follow the change can hold the tracked value; the others matched by coincidence||Each pass writes the new value into every candidate, which forces the real address to reveal itself||The pass looks up the game's source variable names, so the matching address can be labeled||The pass converts temporary heap addresses into permanent ones that stay the same after a restart
5.5.explanation: Each filter pass re-reads only the existing candidates and keeps those that now hold the new value, so unrelated addresses that happened to match once drop out.

5.6.title: Advance by decoded length
5.6.prompt: Why must a disassembler advance by the decoder's reported instruction length?
5.6.options: x86 instructions use a variable number of bytes, so a fixed step would land mid-instruction||Every x86 instruction is four bytes, but the decoder reports the count to save time||Instructions are always aligned to 8-byte boundaries, so the step only has to skip padding||The PE header stores one global instruction size that the decoder reads and reports back
5.6.explanation: Prefixes, opcodes, ModR/M, SIB, displacements, and immediates make x86 instructions variable-length. One wrong boundary corrupts every later decode.

5.7.title: Continue every event
5.7.prompt: What must a minimal Windows debugger do after processing a debug event?
5.7.options: Continue it with a suitable status and close any handles that the event owns||Hold the thread paused until the next event arrives, so the state stays consistent||Rewrite the executable on disk so that the same event cannot fire a second time||Convert the event into a message for the game's own window and wait for its reply
5.7.explanation: Debugging is a protocol with the operating system: every event needs correct handling, continuation, and cleanup. A target whose event is never continued stays frozen.

5.8.title: Keep logging bounded
5.8.prompt: Why should a call logger use a fixed-size or capped buffer?
5.8.options: A hot call site could otherwise eat memory and disturb the program being measured||A cap makes every call unique, so the log never has to store the same call twice||A buffer with a limit stops game threads from running while the log is being written||Logging code needs executable memory, which is only available in fixed-size blocks
5.8.explanation: Instrumentation must control its own cost. Bounded storage, sampling, and dropped-event counters make overhead visible and predictable.

5.9.title: Correlate events over time
5.9.prompt: What makes ETW useful for investigating a short game-performance problem?
5.9.options: Timestamped events from system and application providers can be lined up on one timeline||It pauses every thread at once, so the slow frame can be examined at leisure||It reveals the game's source code, which shows where the slow function was written||It rewrites slow functions automatically, so the stutter disappears in the next run
5.9.explanation: ETW records structured events with timing and provider identity. A short controlled trace helps connect CPU, file, process, and scheduling activity.

5.10.title: Separate scheduling from results
5.10.prompt: Why sort addresses after parallel scanner workers finish?
5.10.options: Worker completion order varies, while a stable result order helps tests and review||Sorting makes an ambiguous pattern unique, so the scanner can accept its result||Windows requires addresses to arrive in ascending order before they are published||Sorting changes the remote pages to read-only, so a later scan cannot disturb them
5.10.explanation: Concurrency may change which worker reports first even when the bytes are identical. Sorting restores deterministic presentation; it does not repair weak evidence or alter the target.

6.1.title: Prove the ABI before calling
6.1.prompt: Which evidence is most important before converting a `GetProcAddress` result into a Rust function pointer?
6.1.options: Argument locations, calling convention, return use, ownership, and behavior seen at several call sites||The export name's spelling, its length, and whether it resembles a documented Windows API name||The numeric size of the returned address and whether it falls inside the DLL's mapped range||The DLL file's version resource, creation date, and the publisher shown in its properties
6.1.explanation: A raw export address has no Rust type. The conversion is sound only when machine evidence and documentation establish the complete call contract.

6.2.title: Respect loader lock
6.2.prompt: Why should `DllMain` do as little work as possible?
6.2.options: Windows calls it while loader bookkeeping is locked, so complex work can deadlock||DLL code cannot allocate memory until the host process has finished starting up||The CPU has no usable stack during process attach, so calls would fault at once||Rust code is not permitted to run inside a DLL entry point on any Windows build
6.2.explanation: Loader notifications run under strict constraints. A small entry point should record state or start a carefully designed next stage, leaving normal work outside loader lock.

6.3.title: Account for separate address spaces
6.3.prompt: Why should an injector avoid assuming that one local function pointer is valid in the target process?
6.3.options: ASLR and architecture differences can give modules different live addresses||Function pointers are stored as text strings that only the owning process can parse||Every process shares one address space, so the pointer is already in use there||Windows removes module exports from memory once the game process starts
6.3.explanation: Processes have separate virtual address spaces. Resolve the target module and export using assumptions proven for that architecture and build.

6.4.title: Treat a patch as a transaction
6.4.prompt: Which sequence makes an in-process detour responsibly reversible?
6.4.options: Verify expected bytes, save originals, write the whole patch, then restore those originals on shutdown||Write the patch first, inspect the result afterward, and rewrite the bytes if anything looks wrong||Patch every address that matches the byte pattern, then restore only the first one at shutdown||Write the patch, then restore it on shutdown by overwriting the span with zero bytes
6.4.explanation: A patch temporarily replaces program state. Verification prevents wrong-build edits, saved bytes enable exact restoration, and whole-instruction boundaries preserve decoding.

6.5.title: Understand the import slot
6.5.prompt: What does an Import Address Table slot normally contain after the loader finishes?
6.5.options: The resolved live address of an imported function||The imported DLL's entire machine code, copied into the executable||The imported function's name as text, kept for the call site to look up||The security token the process uses to call the imported DLL
6.5.explanation: Call sites can load the resolved pointer from the IAT. A reversible lab hook saves that exact pointer, replaces one owned slot, and restores it afterward.

6.6.title: Catch a press that lasts one frame
6.6.prompt: A game draws at 144 frames a second but runs its rules in 60 Hz fixed steps. A key is "just pressed" on frame 4, and frame 4 runs no step. Why can the rules miss the press?
6.6.options: The edge is true for one frame only, so by the frame that runs the next step it is gone||The step reads the keyboard hardware directly, and by then the key has been released||Fixed steps never receive keyboard input, only mouse and controller state||The press is delayed by exactly 60 frames before the step sees it
6.6.explanation: An edge lasts a single frame, and a fixed step is tied to game time, not frames. The usual repair is to queue the press as an intent, such as jump requested, until a step consumes it exactly once.

6.7.title: Choose the actual input path
6.7.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes SendInput from SendMessageW?
6.7.options: SendInput inserts system input events, while SendMessageW calls a window procedure and may be ignored by games using device input||SendMessageW inserts events into the system input stream, while SendInput calls one window's procedure directly and waits||SendInput targets exactly one HWND and bypasses the foreground window, while SendMessageW goes to whichever window has focus||SendMessageW is a stronger form of SendInput because it reaches device state, which Raw Input games read
6.7.explanation: They use different Windows paths. A window message is not a stronger form of device input, and neither API guarantees that a particular game consumes it.

6.8.title: Keep painting separate from side effects
6.8.prompt: Why should an egui menu send an owned Settings command instead of writing game memory directly during every UI frame?
6.8.options: Repainting stays side-effect free, and one worker owns validated handles and cleanup||egui cannot display boolean values unless a worker thread supplies the text for them||Channels make every pointer permanent, so the worker keeps a valid address after unload||A worker thread disables Windows access checks that would block writes from the UI thread
6.8.explanation: Immediate-mode UI runs repeatedly. Sending deliberate snapshots prevents repeated writes and keeps low-level ownership in one reviewable worker.

6.9.title: Make failure isolation last
6.9.prompt: A feature fails during update. The owner logs the error and runs cleanup. What else stops the feature from running again on the next update?
6.9.options: Mark its slot disabled, so the update loop skips it while other features keep running||Keep its enabled flag true, because the logged error already blocks the next update call||Let the input thread rewrite its state directly, so the worker never touches it again||Close every feature's resources at once, so no later update can reach the failed feature
6.9.explanation: Cleanup releases the failing feature’s resources; its disabled slot prevents another update from using them. One owner makes this state change and allows the other enabled features to continue.

6.10.title: Remove a hook without a lifetime race
6.10.prompt: Why enter a Draining phase before restoring bytes and freeing a trampoline?
6.10.options: It stops new callback work and lets active callbacks finish while their code and state are still alive||It rewrites every displaced instruction to one byte, so the trampoline can be freed immediately||It suspends all process threads for good, so nothing can enter the hook after restoration begins||It lets the tool skip saving the original bytes, since the callbacks will restore them themselves
6.10.explanation: Removal is a concurrency transition. Code and callback state must outlive every active user; otherwise a thread can return through memory that has already been released.

7.1.title: Explain perspective division
7.1.prompt: Two equally sized objects have the same orientation. One is twice as far from the camera. Why does it cover roughly half as much screen width?
7.1.options: Projection divides by depth, so doubling depth halves the projected width||The farther object loses half of its vertices, so only half its width gets drawn||Its world coordinates are copied straight to pixels, skipping the camera transform||The camera shrinks the object's real size by half whenever it moves twice as far away
7.1.explanation: The projection carries depth in the homogeneous w component. Dividing by w makes projected size decrease with distance while the object’s world size stays the same.

7.2.title: Trace a graphics decision
7.2.prompt: A render flag is most useful when you can connect it to what?
7.2.options: A conditional branch whose two paths produce different drawing behavior||A writable address that changes value each time the player moves the mouse||The largest parameter value that the OpenGL driver is willing to accept||A file that the game loads at startup and then keeps open for the whole session
7.2.explanation: The flag is data; the branch supplies behavior. Repeatedly toggling one known setting helps prove which code reads it and how rendering changes.

7.3.title: Preserve the call contract
7.3.prompt: What must an observational wrapper around an OpenGL draw call do after recording bounded metadata?
7.3.options: Forward the call with the original calling convention, parameters, and required state||Replace each texture with a plain one first, so that the logged counts are easier to compare||Skip the real draw after logging, so the frame stays unchanged while the sample is saved||Leave the graphics state changed afterwards, so the next call can reuse the same setup
7.3.explanation: A transparent observer preserves the function contract. Otherwise the measurement changes the scene and can no longer be trusted.

7.4.title: Design a visual experiment
7.4.prompt: Why temporarily color one suspected render category at a time?
7.4.options: One controlled change links a recorded call pattern to a visible model group||Each colour reveals the source variable names, so the matching code can be found directly||Setting a colour disables depth testing for that group, which makes the model easier to see||The GPU stores a permanent label with the colour, so the category survives a level reload
7.4.explanation: Changing one reversible thing at a time means any visible difference can come only from the selected rule, so the colored group shows exactly what that rule catches.

7.5.title: Validate the target result
7.5.prompt: Before acting on the game's target-under-crosshair result, what should a tool check?
7.5.options: That the identifier is valid for the current frame and still refers to an allowed target||That the identifier is the highest address seen so far, since newer entities live higher||That the identifier never changes between frames, because a stable value proves validity||That the renderer is paused for the frame, so the game cannot replace the target
7.5.explanation: Selection results are time-sensitive game state. Validate identity, lifetime, and local rules immediately before using them.

7.6.title: Choose a target deliberately
7.6.prompt: Why use an explicit target score instead of selecting the first entity in memory?
7.6.options: Distance, angle, visibility, team, and validity can be weighed by written rules||Memory order follows distance from the crosshair, so a score only repeats that order||The first record is the local player's nearest enemy, by the engine's design||A score lets the client change which targets the server treats as alive
7.6.explanation: An explicit score makes selection predictable, testable, and independent of arbitrary container order.

7.7.title: Model camera motion
7.7.prompt: Why record recoil as a time series instead of one final camera angle?
7.7.options: The samples reveal the impulse, recovery, timing, and damping behavior||A single final angle hides only rounding error, which samples then average away||Time series let you skip the debugger, since each sample names the writing code||The camera only updates once per shot, so extra samples repeat the same value
7.7.explanation: Recoil is a dynamic system. Sampling over time exposes how the game adds an impulse and gradually returns the camera.

7.8.title: Recover the filtering rule
7.8.prompt: What is the best way to infer why one entity appears on radar and another does not?
7.8.options: Compare entities that differ in one property and trace the branch that uses it||Patch each conditional jump in the radar loop until both entities appear||Assume distance is the only rule and measure how far away each one stands||Read the final screen pixels and work backward from the marker colours
7.8.explanation: Controlled comparisons reveal a predicate. Team, visibility, alive state, range, and update timing are candidate inputs that should be tested separately.

7.9.title: Reject points behind the camera
7.9.prompt: Why check clip-space w before the perspective divide?
7.9.options: A zero or negative w can mean the point is on or behind the camera plane||A large w means the point is off-screen, so it must be skipped before dividing||w stores the point's distance in metres, which must be known for range labels||The divide only works when w is exactly 1, so other values are normalized first
7.9.explanation: Dividing blindly can create infinities or mirrored screen coordinates for points that should not be drawn.

7.10.title: Derive the slot
7.10.prompt: `IDXGISwapChain` inherits IUnknown (3 methods), then IDXGIObject (4 methods), then IDXGIDeviceSubObject (1 method), and declares `Present` first. Which vtable index is `Present`, and why does that reasoning matter?
7.10.options: Index 8, because inherited methods come first, so the count can be repeated for any method||Index 0, because Present is the interface's own first method, so it opens the table||Index 3, because IUnknown fills the first three slots and everything else follows at once||Index 8, but only in 32-bit processes, since a 64-bit table is numbered differently
7.10.explanation: 3 + 4 + 1 = 8. The value matters less than the method: counting inherited interfaces in order lets you derive ResizeBuffers, DrawIndexed, or any other slot yourself, and tells you at once when a list found online is describing a different interface. Slot width does change with pointer size, but the index does not.

7.11.title: Count the right thing
7.11.prompt: A filter written for Direct3D 11 keys on `index_count == 900`. Ported to Direct3D 9's `DrawIndexedPrimitive`, it matches nothing. What is the most likely cause?
7.11.options: Direct3D 9 passes a primitive count, so a 900-index triangle list arrives as 300||Direct3D 9 does not support indexed drawing, so the call is never made||The index buffer is bound differently, so Direct3D 9 counts are always zero||Direct3D 9 reports its counts only after the frame has been presented
7.11.explanation: For a triangle list the two differ by a factor of three. Direct3D 11's `DrawIndexed` takes an index count; Direct3D 9's `DrawIndexedPrimitive` takes a primitive count. Confirm which unit an argument carries before porting a threshold, and note that `base_vertex_location` is signed in Direct3D 11 for the same care-with-units reason.

7.12.title: Unify feature inputs
7.12.prompt: Why should several diagnostic features consume one shared frame snapshot?
7.12.options: They use the same captured values and avoid duplicate remote reads||They all receive mutable pointers into the game's own player records||It removes every synchronization problem between the game and the tool||It makes rendering independent of the coordinates stored in the snapshot
7.12.explanation: An owned immutable snapshot gives each feature the same captured values. It does not make a multi-field read atomic: validate the copy and check a tick or generation counter when available.

7.13.title: Pick the hook site
7.13.prompt: You want a menu drawn by the game's own text function. Why is hooking that text function itself the wrong site?
7.13.options: Your hook would call the text function per line, re-entering itself until the stack overflows||The text function runs too rarely to draw a menu, so every line would appear a frame late||Text functions cannot be detoured at all, because they are called through a vtable slot||The menu would be drawn behind the world geometry, where the player could not see it
7.13.explanation: Hook a site that runs once per frame, then call the text function from there as an ordinary function. Lesson 7.9's per-frame print hook is such a site, and drawing there also puts your lines in the same pass as the game's own HUD.

8.1.title: Find the official state
8.1.prompt: In a typical multiplayer design, why can a client-side visual value disagree with the final result?
8.1.options: The server owns the authoritative shared state and resolves outcomes||Packets carry bare timestamps, so each client rebuilds values itself||The GPU applies the game rules before the server sends a reply||The clients share one address space and overwrite each other's values
8.1.explanation: Clients predict and render, while the authoritative server validates and resolves shared outcomes.

8.2.title: Find message structure
8.2.prompt: Which capture method best reveals how one local game action is encoded?
8.2.options: Record a quiet baseline, do one action, then compare changed bytes and timing||Record hours of mixed traffic, then search it for anything that looks unusual||Treat each TCP read in the trace as exactly one application message||Edit the packets in the capture before working out what they mean
8.2.explanation: A controlled capture reduces noise and supports cause-and-effect reasoning. TCP still requires you to infer framing because reads do not preserve application messages.

8.3.title: Preserve message structure
8.3.prompt: What should a safe message rewriter do before changing one field?
8.3.options: Validate framing, lengths, message type, and field bounds first||Overwrite the bytes at a remembered offset without parsing||Assume one read equals one message and patch that read||Drop unknown trailing bytes quietly so the frame looks valid
8.3.explanation: Parsing proves where the field begins and ends; rebuilding must preserve every surrounding protocol rule.

8.4.title: Validate order as well as bytes
8.4.prompt: A chat frame parses correctly but arrives before the protocol greeting. What should the session parser do?
8.4.options: Reject it as an illegal transition for the current state||Accept it, because a clean parse proves the message is legal||Accept it and move the session on to `InLobby` automatically||Reset the frame length to zero and parse the chat again
8.4.explanation: Framing and field parsing prove message shape. A protocol state machine separately decides whether that message is legal at this point in the conversation.

8.5.title: Treat protocol input as untrusted
8.5.prompt: What should a local chat bot do before acting on a decoded command?
8.5.options: Validate framing, size, syntax, and the few allowed commands||Skip the checks, because a loopback lab network is trusted||Use the declared payload length to size its read buffer||Keep references into the receive buffer for later reuse
8.5.explanation: Network data is untrusted even in a lab. Bounded parsing and an explicit command enum keep data from turning into unintended behavior.

8.6.title: Preserve both byte streams
8.6.prompt: What makes a local TCP relay transparent?
8.6.options: It relays both directions, copes with partial I/O and half-closes, and leaves data as is||It calls `recv` once per connection and then leaves the relay running without it||It turns the TCP stream into UDP datagrams to keep the message boundaries intact||It assumes both peers close at the same instant and drops any leftover bytes
8.6.explanation: TCP is a bidirectional stream. Correct relays loop over partial reads/writes and propagate shutdown without inventing message boundaries.

8.7.title: Coordinate shared state
8.7.prompt: Why does shared memory still need a synchronization or publication rule?
8.7.options: A reader could see a new length beside the old payload bytes||Mapped bytes turn read-only for each process that views them||Both processes map the view at one virtual address by rule||A file mapping preserves message boundaries between writes
8.7.explanation: Shared storage does not make a multi-field update atomic. A mutex, event, sequence counter, or carefully designed atomic protocol defines when data is complete.

8.8.title: Separate pipe messages
8.8.prompt: In the lesson's message-mode named pipe, why include a length before the payload?
8.8.options: The receiver can compare the declared size with the bytes received and its limit||The length lets Windows size the pipe buffer on the server's behalf||Message mode drops any write that lacks a length header at the transport level||The length is what switches the pipe from byte mode into message mode
8.8.explanation: Message mode preserves write boundaries in this lab. The length still lets the receiver reject a payload whose declared size differs from the received bytes or exceeds its bound. Stream-mode transports need separate framing to recover application message boundaries.

9.1.title: Choose the simpler data source
9.1.prompt: When is a game file a better analysis target than live process memory?
9.1.options: When the needed state already has a documented or discoverable on-disk format||When the state changes on every CPU instruction and must be sampled live||When the needed values exist only in registers during a single frame||When the game keeps all of its state in anonymous heap pages only
9.1.explanation: Files are stable snapshots that can be copied, diffed, parsed, versioned, and restored. Prefer them when they answer the same question with less moving state.

9.2.title: Avoid a half-written save
9.2.prompt: Which update strategy best protects a save file if the program crashes during writing?
9.2.options: Write and validate a temporary file, then atomically replace the destination||Truncate the save first so the new bytes can be written into the same file||Edit the loaded save in place field by field, flushing after every change||Delete the original, then write the new one under the same file name
9.2.explanation: A temporary file keeps the original intact until a complete replacement is ready. Backups and post-write validation add further recovery points.

9.3.title: Finish the edit
9.3.prompt: You change the gold in a `GSAV` save from 250 to 1,250 with a hex editor, and the game now refuses to load it. What else has to change?
9.3.options: The checksum at offsets 15 to 18, rewritten as the new byte sum 822||The checksum at offsets 15 to 18, rewritten as the new gold value 1,250||Nothing more; the game still holds the old gold value in a cache||The magic number at offsets 0 to 3, since the file's contents changed
9.3.explanation: The loader adds up bytes 0 to 14 and compares the total with the stored checksum. The gold bytes `E2 04 00 00` now add 226 + 4 = 230 instead of 250, so Nia's sum is 842 − 250 + 230 = 822, which has to be written back lowest byte first as `36 03 00 00`.

9.4.title: Preserve the asset contract
9.4.prompt: Why can a visually correct replacement texture still fail to load?
9.4.options: Its dimensions, pixel format, compression, mipmaps, or path may break the engine's expected contract||Its dimensions may match, but the engine still rejects any image edited by a program other than its own tool||Its file name may match, but the engine caches textures by the picture's content and ignores new files||Its colors may be correct, but graphics cards accept only images saved with the original program's palette
9.4.explanation: Asset loaders depend on structure as well as appearance. Match the original metadata and change one property at a time.

9.5.title: Validate structured game data
9.5.prompt: What should a small unit-definition linter check before the game loads the mod?
9.5.options: Required fields, types, ranges, identifiers, and referenced assets||The current memory address of every unit that the file defines||Whether the file is saved in the same text encoding as the base game||Whether each stat line uses the same number as the base game's version
9.5.explanation: A schema turns implicit engine expectations into explicit checks. It catches malformed data before a vague runtime failure.

9.6.title: Keep extraction contained
9.6.prompt: What must be true of every archive entry before a mod installer writes it?
9.6.options: Its validated relative path remains beneath the chosen staging root||Its name already matches a file that exists in the game's folder||Its path uses Windows backslashes, which the installer then converts||Its declared size matches the size shown in the archive's header
9.6.explanation: Absolute paths and parent traversal can escape the destination. Enclosed relative paths plus size and file-type policies keep extraction bounded.

9.7.title: Preserve later work
9.7.prompt: Why should an uninstaller compare the current file with the mod's recorded installed hash?
9.7.options: If it changed later, deleting or restoring blindly would erase newer work||A matching hash is what gives the uninstaller permission to delete files||Comparing hashes lets the installer skip making backups when installing||Hashes record the order in which directories were created by the mod
9.7.explanation: The installed digest is an optimistic concurrency check. A mismatch means the file no longer belongs solely to the recorded mod transaction.

9.8.title: Ask the right trust question
9.8.prompt: What can an Authenticode signature tell you that a standalone SHA-256 hash cannot?
9.8.options: Whether bytes match a publisher's signature under a Windows trust policy||Whether the program has been scanned and has no known vulnerabilities||Whether the file is guaranteed never to be changed by anyone later||Whether every installed antivirus engine has approved the file
9.8.explanation: A hash identifies exact bytes. Authenticode additionally connects a digest to signing identity and certificate policy, without proving the software is bug-free.

9.9.title: Protect the context
9.9.prompt: What does AEAD associated data provide?
9.9.options: Authentication for readable context, such as a slot number and format version||Extra encryption for the context, so a slot number is hidden from viewers||A saved copy of the key, kept beside the ciphertext for later recovery||A compressed form of the ciphertext, which shortens a very large save
9.9.explanation: Associated data remains visible but is covered by authentication, so changing the context makes decryption fail.

10.1.title: Find the authority
10.1.prompt: In an embedded Lua design, who decides which game operations a script can request?
10.1.options: The compiled host that builds the script API||The Lua interpreter, which picks functions by script name||The script file, through its first line of code||The operating system, from the file's extension
10.1.explanation: The host owns the interpreter and chooses which functions and values enter the environment, making that API the capability boundary. The interpreter only runs what it is given.

10.2.title: Translate the index
10.2.prompt: Rust vector element `0` becomes which conventional Lua sequence key?
10.2.explanation: Rust collections are zero-indexed while Lua sequences conventionally start at one, so the host adds one during conversion.

10.3.title: Load only what is needed
10.3.prompt: Why does the Rust host load table, string, and math libraries but omit Lua's I/O, OS, debug, and package libraries?
10.3.options: The scripts get a smaller, documented set of capabilities||Lua requires exactly three libraries to start running||The omitted libraries are not really part of Lua||Leaving them out makes scripts compile as Rust code
10.3.explanation: Library selection does not create a complete sandbox, but it avoids granting unrelated filesystem, process, debugging, or module-loading capabilities.

10.4.title: Keep pointers in Rust
10.4.prompt: Why should a Lua observer receive copied entity snapshots rather than target-process addresses?
10.4.options: Rust owns layout validation, and scripts cannot keep stale pointers||Lua cannot store integers large enough for addresses||Snapshots stay identical forever, so scripts never need updates||Pointers only work for programs that talk over a network
10.4.explanation: A domain snapshot keeps architecture, permissions, bounds, and lifetimes inside the typed host while giving scripts the meaning they need.

10.5.title: Wait for confirmation
10.5.prompt: After a Lua bot requests one action, why should it enter a wait state?
10.5.options: To observe confirmation or timeout before asking again||Lua can execute only one function per script run||The snapshot becomes writable during the wait||Waiting changes the calling convention of the request
10.5.explanation: A pending state prevents duplicate input and makes success, failure, cancellation, and timeout explicit.

10.6.title: Limit different resources
10.6.prompt: Why is an instruction budget not a complete Lua sandbox?
10.6.options: Memory, time, callbacks, and actions need own limits||Lua instructions never run inside a hosted script||The hook itself grants the script file access too||A budget turns off every kind of script error
10.6.explanation: Instruction hooks address runaway bytecode. A robust host layers limited libraries, bounded callbacks, memory and time limits, validation, and cancellation.

10.7.title: Why a budget, not a prediction?
10.7.prompt: A game's Lua host runs scripts from downloaded mods. Why does it stop any script after a fixed number of steps instead of first checking whether the script will ever finish?
10.7.options: No program can decide whether all scripts halt||Checking is possible, but it is too slow on older machines||Lua scripts cannot loop forever, so the budget saves memory||A step budget makes each script finish sooner than before
10.7.explanation: This is the halting problem in practice. A checker that always correctly predicts whether a program halts cannot exist, because a program built to do the opposite of the checker's answer makes every answer wrong. So a host does not try to predict. It counts steps inside the execution loop and stops a script that runs past its budget, exactly as Lesson 10.8's VM loop does.

10.8.title: Follow the virtual machine
10.8.prompt: What does the tiny Lua VM's instruction pointer identify?
10.8.options: The next bytecode instruction||The next x86 instruction in Windows||The first table key in memory||The heap memory left over
10.8.explanation: The processor has a native instruction pointer, while an interpreter keeps a separate index into its bytecode program.

10.9.title: Find the lifetime problem
10.9.prompt: Why can plain strong reference counting leak two Lua tables that point to each other?
10.9.options: Each keeps the other's count above zero||Tables cannot hold other tables inside them||Reference counts can only be kept for strings||Lua never frees a value once it is created
10.9.explanation: A cycle can keep its own strong counts alive. A tracing collector or another cycle strategy is needed for a general interpreter.

10.10.title: Let a local escape
10.10.prompt: What must happen to an upvalue that still refers to a local when the local's call frame returns?
10.10.options: It moves into storage owned by the closure||It turns into a raw pointer to the stack||It is deleted along with every closure||It becomes a global string value
10.10.explanation: Closing the upvalue preserves the captured value after its original stack slot stops belonging to an active frame.

11.1.title: Separate file from execution
11.1.prompt: Which item exists only after Windows creates a running process?
11.1.options: A virtual address space with threads, handles, stacks, and mapped modules||The PE section table, import list, and entry-point RVA stored in the file||The executable's bytes and checksum sitting on disk before launch||The filename, extension, and version resource shown in Explorer
11.1.explanation: A program file is input to process creation. Windows maps it, resolves imports, creates execution state, and adds private memory not present on disk.

11.2.title: Which collector moves objects?
11.2.prompt: Two games are both described as 'managed and garbage collected': one is Unity on the Mono backend, the other runs on .NET CoreCLR. Which statement is accurate?
11.2.options: Unity's non-compacting collector leaves survivors in place; CoreCLR's compacting one can relocate them||Both collectors compact the heap on each collection, so no managed address survives one||Neither collector moves survivors, so addresses behave exactly as they would in a native game||Older 32-bit runtimes relocate objects, so a 64-bit game of either kind keeps stable addresses
11.2.explanation: 'Managed' does not decide whether an address is durable; the specific collector does. Unity's Mono does not move survivors, so fixed addresses behave much as in native games. CoreCLR relocates survivors, so there you need a stable reference such as a handle or a re-lookup.

11.3.title: Tie offsets to exact bytes
11.3.prompt: Why does a patcher keep an executable's SHA-256 digest next to the RVAs and byte patterns it uses?
11.3.options: So the patch can refuse to apply when the target build's bytes differ||So the digest can lock the file against being replaced by a game update||So the hash can hide the patched address from ASLR when the module loads||So the digest can grant the tool the process rights it needs to write
11.3.explanation: RVAs and byte patterns belong to one compiled build. The digest identifies the exact file they came from, so a mismatch stops the patch before it writes into different code.

11.4.title: Accept a recovered field carefully
11.4.prompt: Which checks most strongly support an offset as a health field in a new build?
11.4.options: A damage path stores there, controlled changes match, range relations hold, and identity is stable across restarts||The offset holds one small integer, a scan found it once, and it sits near the old build's health offset||A memory viewer shows it as green, one scan hit has the right value, and it is close to the old offset||The same number appears there in two snapshots, a scan for 100 returned it, and the page is writable
11.4.explanation: Independent static, dynamic, relational, and identity checks cross-validate the field. One plausible number is only a candidate.

11.5.title: Request the smallest capability
11.5.prompt: A tool only needs to list a process's mapped regions. What access principle should guide `OpenProcess`?
11.5.options: Request only the query rights that this one operation needs||Request full access once, then drop the unneeded rights after the first call||Request read and write rights so one handle covers every later feature||Request the rights of the highest-integrity process so the DACL permits it
11.5.explanation: Least privilege narrows accidental capability, documents intent, and makes failures easier to reason about. Rights cannot be quietly dropped later, since they are recorded on the handle.

11.6.title: Prevent resource leaks
11.6.prompt: What invariant should a safe wrapper maintain for an owned Windows handle?
11.6.options: Exactly one owner closes a valid handle exactly once||Every function that receives the handle closes it when finished||The numeric handle value stays fixed until the process exits||The handle stays open until Windows shuts down, so none can reuse it
11.6.explanation: Single ownership prevents both leaks and double-close bugs. Borrowed handles need a different type because they do not own cleanup.

11.7.title: Read the map before the bytes
11.7.prompt: What does a virtual-memory region query tell an observer before it reads?
11.7.options: Whether the range is committed, plus its current protection and type||Which game objects live in the range and the source names of their fields||Whether the bytes in the range changed since the last scan of this process||Which thread most recently wrote into the range and the time it did so
11.7.explanation: Region metadata lets the tool skip unmapped, guarded, or inappropriate pages and report why. It describes the pages but does not copy their bytes.

11.8.title: Read execution state
11.8.prompt: What does a captured thread context describe?
11.8.options: Register state, including the current instruction and stack locations||Every instruction the thread will execute from this point until it exits||The thread's name, base priority, and the command line of its process||A copy of the process's address space as this thread currently sees it
11.8.explanation: A context is one instant of CPU-visible thread state. Combining it with stack memory and module symbols helps reconstruct active calls.

11.9.title: Follow the abstraction layers
11.9.prompt: What happens conceptually when a user-mode API needs the Windows kernel to perform privileged work?
11.9.options: A controlled system-call transition enters a kernel service, then returns to user mode||The caller becomes a kernel thread and keeps kernel privileges until the process exits||The process maps all kernel memory into its address space and edits it directly||The API rewrites the executable on disk so its code runs with kernel privileges
11.9.explanation: Win32 and native API layers prepare arguments before a processor-supported privilege transition reaches a kernel service. The boundary is controlled, not a shared address space.

11.10.title: Why programs cannot jump into the kernel
11.10.prompt: A user-mode program knows the virtual address of the kernel's `NtReadVirtualMemory`. Why can it not simply call that address and skip the checks at the kernel's system-call entry?
11.10.options: Kernel pages are supervisor-only or absent for ring 3, so a plain call faults; only `syscall` enters the kernel safely||It can, and that is exactly why Windows keeps its system service numbers hidden from ordinary programs||The kernel moves its routines to a new random address every second, so any stored address is almost always stale||The call would run, but the kernel later discards any request whose return address is outside `ntdll.dll`
11.10.explanation: Kernel mappings are supervisor-only, or omitted from the user page table. Either way, ring 3 cannot fetch their instructions through an ordinary call. A configured system-call entry transfers execution to an entry point the kernel prepared; the kernel then validates the request and access rights. Service numbers are identifiers, not secrets.

11.11.title: Why the kernel checks addresses itself
11.11.prompt: Kernel pages have their user/supervisor bit cleared, so ring-3 code faults if it touches them. Why must the kernel's `NtReadVirtualMemory` still check that the requested range and the caller's buffer lie in user space?
11.11.options: The copy runs in ring 0, where supervisor pages are allowed, so an unchecked range could expose kernel memory||The check is needed only for 32-bit programs that arrive through WoW64, since their shorter pointers can overflow||The user/supervisor bit is consulted only when code is fetched, never when data is read, so data copies need a check||The check speeds the copy up by letting the kernel skip page-table walks for ranges already known to be in user space
11.11.explanation: The user/supervisor bit stops code running at ring 3. The copy itself runs in ring 0, inside the kernel, where the processor allows access to supervisor pages. If the kernel accepted a range in its own half of the address space, or one long enough to wrap around to a small address, it would copy kernel memory out to the caller or write the caller's bytes over kernel memory. So the kernel checks every address that user mode hands it before using it.

11.12.title: Interpret a crash dump
11.12.options: A selected snapshot of process state, such as threads, modules, and registers, captured at one moment||A live connection to a running process that streams its threads and registers as they change||A complete copy of the whole game installation folder, saved so it can be restored later||A debugger breakpoint stored in hardware, which pauses the process again whenever it is opened
11.12.explanation: Dump contents depend on capture flags. Threads, modules, contexts, and chosen memory ranges describe the captured instant, not future execution.

12.1.title: Explain a changed module list
12.1.prompt: A new DLL appears in a game's module inventory. What should you check first?
12.1.options: Its full path, hash, signer or source, load timing, and whether the baseline expected it||Remove it from the folder right away, because any module missing from the baseline is a threat||Trust its short filename, since the name is the part of identity that Windows verifies||Patch its entry point so the loader skips it the next time the game starts up
12.1.explanation: Different files can share one short module name. The full path, the hash of the exact bytes, the signer, and a comparison with the approved baseline show which file was loaded and whether the baseline expected it.

12.2.title: Avoid startup deadlocks
12.2.prompt: Why is loading another DLL or waiting for worker synchronization dangerous inside `DllMain`?
12.2.options: The loader may already hold locks that a nested operation or worker needs, forming a cycle||DLLs have no access to synchronization objects, so any wait inside `DllMain` fails at once||Threads cannot exist in a process while a DLL is attaching, so any wait there never ends||The PE format forbids any function call during start-up, so such a call makes the loader abort
12.2.explanation: Waiting or re-entering loader work while loader lock is held can create a circular dependency. Keep notifications minimal and initialize later.

12.3.title: Treat absence as a state
12.3.prompt: What should a runtime API resolver do when an optional export is not present?
12.3.options: Return `None` and use the documented lower-capability fallback||Call address zero, which Windows treats as a request to use the nearest older function instead||Guess a similarly named export, since exports in one DLL usually share the same signature||Patch the system DLL so the missing export exists, then call it as if it had been there
12.3.explanation: Optional lookup needs an explicit missing case. A known fallback preserves compatibility without inventing a function contract.

12.4.title: Registers are not memory
12.4.prompt: A developer adds a debugging line to the toy keypad's driver that reads the DATA register every millisecond “just to display it.” What goes wrong?
12.4.options: Each read removes the event it returns, so key presses shown in the log never reach the program waiting in `ReadFile`||Nothing, because reading a register never changes the device, and the extra reads only cost a little processor time||Every read raises the interrupt line again, so the interrupt service routine runs over and over without stopping||The processor caches the register on the first read, so the log shows the same value forever and misses new keys
12.4.explanation: Reading DATA hands over the front event and removes it from the device's queue, so the debugging read and the DPC compete for events and the log wins some of them. Register reads can have side effects, which is why they are never cached or skipped, why only the owning driver touches them, and why the DPC reads DATA exactly once per event.

12.5.title: What the access bits protect
12.5.prompt: A driver defines a control code that writes to its device, with the access bits (bits 14 and 15) set to `00`. Which programs can send it?
12.5.options: Any program that can open a handle to the device, since access `00` means the I/O manager requires no particular rights||Only programs whose handle holds write access, since the command writes to the device and so needs that right||Only the driver's own service, since control codes are private to the driver that defines them in its code||None at all, since access `00` marks the command as disabled until the driver sets a different value
12.5.explanation: The I/O manager compares a control code's access bits with the rights on the caller's handle before the driver runs. `00` means any access, so the check passes for every handle. A command that changes the device should declare write access, `10`, so that only handles opened for writing can send it. Powerful commands declared with access `00` are one of the classic driver mistakes that attackers look for.

12.6.title: Respect privilege boundaries
12.6.prompt: Why do ordinary game-analysis labs stay in user mode?
12.6.options: A user-mode mistake is contained more narrowly than a failure in a privileged driver||User mode has no access controls, so a mistake there can never reach another process||Kernel code cannot inspect memory, so a mistake there would only affect the driver||Drivers automatically make experiments reproducible, so the lab would not need a reset
12.6.explanation: Kernel code shares system-wide privilege and failure impact. User mode provides a safer boundary for learning, testing, and recovery.

12.7.title: Choose the right map
12.7.prompt: Why is a process virtual pointer not automatically an offset in a physical RAM capture?
12.7.options: Page tables translate each address space's virtual pages to physical locations||A capture is sorted by process ID, so virtual pointers act as keys into that list||Virtual pointers are always 32-bit, too small to index a full RAM image||Physical RAM has no addresses of its own, only process pointers do
12.7.explanation: The capture is organized by physical address. The matching CR3 and page tables connect a process's virtual address to that physical location.

12.8.title: Read across a boundary
12.8.prompt: Why must a virtual-memory reader translate again after crossing a page boundary?
12.8.options: The next virtual page may map to a completely different physical page||Each page uses its own CPU architecture, so the walk must restart||The CR3 register changes after every 4,096 bytes are read||Page boundaries mark where the capture file ends for that process
12.8.explanation: Virtual adjacency does not guarantee physical adjacency. Each crossed page needs its own validated translation.

12.9.title: Check more than one field
12.9.prompt: A capture reader decodes a player object and its health field reads 100. What makes the decoded object trustworthy?
12.9.options: Provenance matches, the identity path is confirmed, and independent invariants hold||The decoded address is a large number, so it points deep into real game data pages||The capture file has a short name, so it was recorded by the standard lab tool||The hexdump output is colored, which marks each byte as validated by the reader tool
12.9.explanation: A wrong CR3 or stale pointer can still lead to a valid-looking object. Confirm the capture and process identity, the expected path to this entity, and its generation as well as independent field relationships. Two agreeing translators establish the translation, not the intended object's identity.

13.1.title: Guard the copy that decides
13.1.prompt: A heal command is checked against the health bar's cached value, then applied to the simulation's entity object. Why can an out-of-range heal still get through?
13.1.options: The check ran on one copy and the change hit another, so the deciding copy went unchecked||The cache stores health in hexadecimal, which breaks the comparison for large values in it||Health bars refresh too slowly, so the displayed change arrives after the heal is applied to it||A control only works when a detector is also running next to it in the game at the time
13.1.explanation: A control protects only the copy it runs against. The authoritative copy is the one whose value decides what happens next, so the range check belongs where that copy changes.

13.2.title: Detect a control contradiction
13.2.prompt: Which event pair directly contradicts a guarded-operation invariant?
13.2.options: A denied decision followed by a changed effect with the same correlation ID||Two ordinary snapshots with different timestamps and the same generation||An allowed decision followed by an unchanged optional effect and a postcondition||A queue reporting zero dropped events during the analyzed interval
13.2.explanation: A shared correlation ID connects the refusal to the effect. If state changes anyway, the decision and effect boundary disagree.

13.3.title: Check what the effect consumes
13.3.prompt: A checksum validates a display cache, but the guarded operation changes a separate simulation object. What is the central design failure?
13.3.options: The check and the effect use different sources of truth||The checksum is stored in hexadecimal, which hides mismatches in the record||The display cache lives in RAM, where its bytes can change at any time||The operation returns an enum, which makes the verification result ambiguous
