13.3.explanation: An integrity result must describe the same identity and state consumed by the effect. A valid copy does not prove that a different canonical object is valid or fresh.

13.4.title: Interpret an environmental signal
13.4.prompt: Why is one long timing sample weak evidence of debugger activity?
13.4.options: Preemption, power management, virtualization, page faults, and load can cause the delay||Monotonic clocks cannot measure elapsed time, so every sample is unreliable by design||A debugger always makes execution faster, so a long delay must point to something else||Timing samples carry no numbers, so a single one cannot be compared with any limit
13.4.explanation: A delay is a signal, not intent. A measured baseline, repeated samples, explicit state transitions, and independent game-state validation make the result interpretable.

13.5.title: Invert the transform
13.5.prompt: The encoder computes `(value ^ key).rotate_left(7)`. Which decoder restores the value?
13.5.explanation: Invert a composition in reverse order: undo the left rotation with a right rotation, then undo XOR by applying the same key again.

13.6.title: Repair the shared effect
13.6.prompt: A read-only toy policy blocks WriteMemory but accepts ApplyPatch even though both change state. What is the strongest repair?
13.6.options: Classify commands by effect and authorize the shared boundary||Add one more forbidden command name to the policy's blocked list, then retest||Hide ApplyPatch from the menu so that users cannot choose that command any more||Log only the commands that were successfully executed by the lab each time
13.6.explanation: Names are inputs; the protected invariant belongs at the common effect. An exhaustive enum match and regression test keep new state-changing variants covered.

13.7.title: Repair the property, not the proxy
13.7.prompt: A health command is accepted whenever an observer flag is absent, even when health exceeds its maximum. What is the strongest repair?
13.7.options: Validate the health range at the effect boundary; record the signal separately||Add a second spelling for the observer flag so that both forms are refused as well||Hide the health field from the menu so that players can no longer reach it at all||Increase the timing threshold so that the observer flag fires much less often than now
13.7.explanation: The environment signal is only diagnostic evidence. The health relation belongs at the state-changing boundary and must hold whether the signal is present or absent.

13.8.title: Count the outcomes
13.8.prompt: An asset gate calls `verify(...)` which returns `Result<bool, VerifyError>`, then uses `.unwrap_or(true)`. Why does this weaken the control more than a weak hash would?
13.8.options: It turns 'verification could not run' into 'verification passed', so breaking the manifest is easier than forging a file||It makes the hash comparison run twice, so a damaged manifest only slows loading and never lets a bad asset through||It rejects every asset whose hash is unknown, so an attacker mostly needs to guess the manifest's file name||It hides hash mismatches from the log, although a mismatching asset is still blocked from loading
13.8.explanation: There are three outcomes, not two: matched, did not match, and could not tell. Folding the error case into success means an attacker can delete, lock, or truncate the manifest instead of defeating the hash. Fail closed, and keep the unavailable case distinct from the mismatch case so a human can tell a changed file from broken verification.

14.1.title: What memory integrity still prevents
14.1.prompt: Memory integrity is on, and an attacker exploits a driver bug that lets them write to any kernel data page. Why can they still not run new code of their own in the kernel?
14.1.options: Stage 2 is the hypervisor's, never lets a page be writable and executable, and only VTL1 grants execute after a signature check||Kernel data pages are encrypted with a key held in VTL1, so any injected bytes decode into meaningless instructions||The kernel rereads its own code every second and repairs any changed instruction from a signed backup copy||Memory writes from drivers are refused by the processor while memory integrity is on, so kernel data cannot change either
14.1.explanation: Ring-0 code in VTL0 controls the stage-1 page tables but not stage 2, which belongs to the hypervisor. With memory integrity on, a page becomes executable in stage 2 only after the secure kernel in VTL1 has verified its code, and executable pages are never writable. The attacker can corrupt data, but cannot write into code pages or turn a data page into code.

14.2.title: Why trap and emulate failed on x86
14.2.prompt: Before VT-x and AMD-V, why could a hypervisor not simply run a guest kernel in ring 3 and emulate each privileged instruction when it faulted?
14.2.options: Instructions like `popf` quietly act differently in ring 3 and never fault, so the hypervisor never sees them||Code in ring 3 runs several times slower than ring 0 code, so a guest kernel there was unusably slow||A guest kernel checks its own ring at start-up and refuses to boot anywhere except ring 0||Processors could raise a fault from ring 3 only for memory accesses, never for privileged instructions
14.2.explanation: Trap and emulate needs every sensitive instruction to fault outside the most privileged level, so that the hypervisor gets control. In ring 3, `popf` leaves the interrupt flag alone without faulting, so a guest kernel that used it to switch interrupts on would carry on believing they were on while nothing told the hypervisor. VMware rewrote such instructions with binary translation, Xen changed the guest kernel's source, and VT-x and AMD-V later gave guests their own ring 0.

14.3.title: Two parts of a working image
14.3.prompt: A firmware image uses the right Cortex-M CPU target but a memory.x file for a different board. Is matching the CPU enough to make the image correct?
14.3.options: No: the target picks instructions, but the linker layout must match the board's addresses and sizes||Yes: every Cortex-M board shares one memory map, so the CPU target alone fixes the whole layout||Yes: QEMU replaces a physical board's memory map automatically when the image is first loaded||No: firmware must run inside a guest OS, and that OS supplies the layout for the board
14.3.explanation: The CPU target and board layout answer different questions. A board can have the same instruction set but different flash/RAM addresses, capacities, pin assignments and peripherals. Firmware must match those details, and its runtime/startup arrangement must match how that board boots.

14.4.title: Why not just ask?
14.4.prompt: Why can an online service not simply ask a console whether its software has been modified?
14.4.options: Modified software could answer "no", so the service needs a signed report from the security processor||Consoles cannot send any message at all before the owner has signed in to an account||The honest answer would be too large to send, so the console sends a short random number||Online services may not ask consoles about their software, so they ban unlisted consoles instead
14.4.explanation: Any answer that software produces, modified software can produce too. Remote attestation works because the signing key sits in the security processor, where software cannot read it, and because each boot stage recorded a hash of the next stage before running it. A console that booted modified software cannot produce a report that both carries a valid signature and matches the known-good measurements.

14.5.title: Lock the port, keep the repair bench
14.5.prompt: A device maker wants its own failure-analysis lab to be able to debug returned units, and nobody else. Which design does that?
14.5.options: Keep it locked; open it only for a signature over a fresh nonce and the unit's ID||Leave the JTAG header off the board, so nobody outside the lab can reach the port||Protect the port with a password printed in the service manual, the same for every unit||Blow a fuse on every unit that disables debug permanently once it has left the factory
14.5.explanation: The nonce is new for every attempt, so a recorded answer fails. Including the unit's ID makes each answer good for one unit only. The private key never leaves the maker, so knowing how the protocol works does not let anyone forge an answer. A missing header only adds effort, a shared password leaks once and then opens every unit, and a permanent fuse locks out the maker's own lab as well.

14.6.title: Reading a board you know nothing about
14.6.prompt: A debugger resets the scan chain of a board it knows nothing about and scans out the data registers. How can it tell where each chip's answer begins, without knowing any chip's register lengths?
14.6.options: An IDCODE chip starts with a 1 and then 31 more bits; a BYPASS chip sends just a 0||Every chip sends its name as text after reset, ending with a zero byte, so the debugger reads to each zero||The debugger times how long each chip takes to answer on TDO and splits the bits at the pauses||The TAP controller counts the chips during reset and sends the total first, then one ID each
14.6.explanation: IDCODEs come out lowest bit first, and bit 0 of every IDCODE is fixed at 1, while a bypass register always captures 0. So each chip's first bit tells the debugger what follows: a 1 starts a 32-bit ID, so the next 31 bits belong to the same chip; a 0 is a chip without IDCODE, which contributes that single bit. Reading bit by bit walks the whole chain, starting with the chip nearest TDO.

14.7.title: Why cheat codes are just addresses
14.7.prompt: Why can a cheat code for an old console game be as simple as “write 99 to address 0x80 every frame”, while a tool for a PC game usually needs a pointer path?
14.7.options: One fixed memory map with no virtual memory or ASLR keeps each variable at the same address||Console games store every value twice, once in RAM and once in a shadow copy for cheats||Emulators translate each guest address into a PC address that never changes between runs||Old consoles encrypted their RAM, so only a few fixed addresses could ever be read out
14.7.explanation: Windows gives each process its own virtual address space and places modules and heap allocations differently between runs (Lesson 2.7), so a PC tool has to rediscover values through pointer paths. An old console has fixed RAM at fixed addresses, and its games lay their variables out the same way every time, so an address found once stays valid, and a cheat is just an address and a value.

14.8.title: Paying back the overshoot
14.8.prompt: The toy console's frame budget is 18 cycles. A frame stops at 19 cycles, because the instruction that crossed the budget could not stop halfway. Why does the emulator give the next frame 17 cycles instead of 18?
14.8.options: Taking off the 1-cycle overshoot keeps the average at exactly 18 per frame, so speed stays right||The CPU runs faster in the second frame, so it needs fewer cycles to do the same work||17 cycles is the most any frame can use without overshooting, so it becomes every budget||The save state taken at the frame boundary uses up one cycle of the next frame
14.8.explanation: An instruction always runs to its end, so a frame can pass its budget: here step 8, an ADD worth 2 cycles, started at 17 and finished at 19. If every frame then got a fresh 18, the extra cycles would pile up and the emulated machine would run ahead of real time. Subtracting each overshoot from the next budget cancels it, so over many frames the average is exactly 18.

8.9.title: Keep newer input during correction
8.9.prompt: The server acknowledges command 3 at position 2. Command 4, a move of minus one, is still pending. How should the client reconcile?
8.9.options: Start at position 2 and replay only command 4||Start at position 2 and replay commands 1 through 4||Keep its old position and remove all four commands||Start at position 2 and wait before showing command 4
8.9.explanation: The acknowledged state already includes commands 1 through 3. Only command 4 remains unacknowledged. Replaying its minus-one displacement gives 2 minus 1, or position 1, without repeating accepted input.

15.1.title: Who owns the reward?
15.1.prompt: A client claims score 99 in the toy world. The server has score 3 and one available one-point coin. What should determine the final score?
15.1.options: The server validates the pickup and awards its one-point reward||The server accepts the claimed total after authenticating the player||The server averages its total with the client's claimed total||The server trusts the newest total if its packet arrived intact
15.1.explanation: The server owns the available coin and reward. A permitted pickup changes 3 to 4; authentication and packet integrity do not make a claimed score authoritative.

15.2.title: Before the position is sent
15.2.prompt: The server knows an enemy position that this observer is not entitled to see. Which design protects that information boundary?
15.2.options: Exclude that position from this client's outgoing observation||Include the position but omit its visible drawing||Include the position only in an encrypted game connection||Include the position and ask the client to hide it
15.2.explanation: Information retained in the client can be observed there. The server constructs a permitted observation before sending it, while handling legitimate visibility and latency needs.

15.3.title: Read the measurement correctly
15.3.prompt: A weighted measurement uses (old times 9 plus sample) divided by 10. Starting from 0.5, a new sample of 1 gives which value?
15.3.options: 0.55, preserving nine-tenths of the previous measurement||0.50, preserving the previous measurement without change||0.60, adding one-tenth directly to the previous measurement||1.00, replacing the previous measurement with the latest sample
15.3.explanation: Nine times 0.5 is 4.5. Add 1 to get 5.5, then divide by 10 to get 0.55. This is weighted history, not a ratio over a fixed last-fifteen window.

15.4.title: A valid signature has limits
15.4.prompt: Why can the loading policy refuse a signed driver in this lesson's fixture?
15.4.options: Its identity matches the known vulnerable-driver blocklist||Its signature guarantees safety only in ordinary user mode||Its signature expires whenever a protected game starts||Its kernel role makes every publisher signature invalid
15.4.explanation: A valid signature does not prove bug-free code. A separate policy can block an identified vulnerable driver. Blocklist maintenance and compatibility testing still matter.

15.5.title: Count the flagged group
15.5.prompt: In the hypothetical population, 99 cheaters and 999 honest players are flagged. About what fraction of the flagged group cheats?
15.5.options: 9 percent of the flagged group||99 percent of the flagged group||90 percent of the flagged group||1 percent of the flagged group
15.5.explanation: The group has 99 plus 999, or 1,098 people. Dividing 99 by 1,098 gives about 0.0902, or 9 percent. Catching 99 percent of cheaters measures recall, not precision.

15.6.title: Follow event identity
15.6.prompt: Game logging, a plugin, and a report describe event A. A later record describes event B. How many distinct events does the ledger contain?
15.6.options: Two events, after merging the three reports about A||Four events, because each notification supplies another event||Three events, after ignoring the later report about B||One event, because all reports concern the same player
15.6.explanation: Three notifications about A still describe one event. B adds another. Distinct events do not automatically establish statistical independence or guilt.

15.7.title: Privilege and information
15.7.prompt: The server excludes a hidden enemy position from the client update. What does observing that received client memory reveal?
15.7.options: Only delivered data; the excluded position is absent||All server data, if the observer has kernel privilege||All server data, if a device can access client memory||The excluded position, if the client hides its drawing
15.7.explanation: Greater local access does not create a value never delivered. Other channels must also be checked, and server validation remains necessary.

15.8.title: Separate lifetime from privilege
15.8.prompt: What does the checked June 2026 Vanguard announcement change for sufficiently secured PCs that opt in?
15.8.options: It permits protection to start with a Riot game||It removes every kernel component from Vanguard protection||It gives every installation the same mandatory boot lifetime||It makes server validation unnecessary for protected sessions
15.8.explanation: Riot announced an optional on-demand mode on qualifying secured PCs. Traditional boot-managed operation remains a different mode; privilege and lifetime are separate properties.

15.9.title: One reward for one object
15.9.prompt: The server has already committed pickup C and score 1. The same request arrives again after a reply was lost. What preserves the invariant?
15.9.options: Return the committed result without adding another reward||Add another reward because the session is authenticated||Restore the coin before processing the repeated request||Ban the sender because every repeated request proves cheating
15.9.explanation: Idempotence preserves one effect across repeated delivery. The coin and reward were committed together. A normal retry gets the recorded result while score stays 1.

1.10.prompt: A byte has bits 2 and 0 set. How does their position produce its unsigned value?
1.10.options: Add their weights, four and one.||Count their names as decimal digits.||Multiply the bit count by eight.||Read the positions as two addresses.
1.10.explanation: Position i contributes 2 to the power i when set. Positions 2 and 0 contribute 4 and 1, giving 5.
1.10.title: Explore the concept

2.11.title: Copy without consuming
2.11.prompt: A game copies an ammo count from one register into another. What happens to the original register?
2.11.options: It keeps its value while the destination receives a copy||It becomes zero once the destination receives the count||It becomes an address pointing at the destination register||It loses its type until the game reads the ammo field again
2.11.explanation: An ordinary register copy writes the destination without consuming or clearing the source. The same value can remain in both registers.

2.12.title: Compare before changing
2.12.prompt: A shop checks a gold amount against a cost using a comparison. What changes during that comparison alone?
2.12.options: The comparison flags change while the gold value stays put||The gold value changes while the comparison flags stay put||Both gold and price become the subtraction result together||The return address becomes the cost of the selected purchase
2.12.explanation: An integer comparison computes subtraction flags and discards the numeric difference. Spending requires a separate write or arithmetic update.

2.13.title: Read the low scalar value
2.13.prompt: A scalar single-precision operation uses an XMM register. How much of that register holds the numeric value being calculated?
2.13.options: One low 32-bit float inside the wider register storage||One 128-bit integer using every bit of the register storage||Four 32-bit floats that must all change on every scalar step||One pointer whose address selects the floating-point format
2.13.explanation: Scalar single-precision operations calculate one binary32 value in the low 32 bits. The rest of the 128-bit XMM register still exists and follows that instruction form's rules.

1.11.title: Reason about the concept
1.11.prompt: A lookup may return no value. A calculation should run only when a value exists. What does mapping the optional value do?
1.11.options: Replace an absent value with the smallest number.||Run the calculation once for every possible value.||Convert all calculation failures into absent data.||Transform the contained value, preserving absence.
1.11.explanation: Mapping changes a present value; absence skips the transformation and remains absent.

1.12.title: Reason about the concept
1.12.prompt: An iterator chain filters and transforms items. Nothing consumes the chain yet. What is normally happening?
1.12.options: Operations are described; item processing is deferred.||All operations have finished and saved their output.||Only the final item has already been transformed.||The source collection has been cleared for reuse.
1.12.explanation: Iterator adaptors are generally lazy. A consumer requests items and drives the chain.

1.13.title: Reason about the concept
1.13.prompt: A returned slice points into the caller’s buffer. What does a matching lifetime annotation express?
1.13.options: The annotation keeps the buffer alive indefinitely.||The returned borrow is tied to the input borrow.||The returned slice owns a separate copied buffer.||The annotation specifies a duration in milliseconds.
1.13.explanation: A lifetime describes validity relationships; it does not allocate or extend storage.

1.14.title: Reason about the concept
1.14.prompt: A guard owns a saved local value and a temporary replacement. Where can it centralize restoration?
1.14.options: A hidden retry inside every successful calculation.||A copied numeric field in every unrelated caller.||Its Drop implementation at ordinary scope exit.||A comment placed beside the first temporary write.
1.14.explanation: The guard pairs acquisition with a cleanup duty that follows its ownership scope.
